client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away two months ago. Every time there's a family get-together, I just can't seem to enjoy it the way I used to — it's like this heavy sadness just takes over and I can't shake it. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for giving this a try — that takes courage, especially when you're carrying something this heavy. Losing your grandmother and then facing those family gatherings without her sounds incredibly painful, like the joy has a shadow over it now. I'm curious — when you say you're not sure talking will change anything, is that a feeling that's been with you for a while, or is it more something that's come up since losing her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I've always been a little skeptical about therapy — like, what's talking going to do when the problem is just that she's gone and nothing can change that? But I think it's gotten worse since she passed, because it just feels so permanent and final, and I don't see how any amount of conversation fixes that. I guess I'm just scared that I'll sit here, talk about it, feel sad, and then go home feeling exactly the same.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — you're not wrong that talking can't bring her back, and it would feel hollow if I promised otherwise. What therapy can sometimes do is help you carry the weight differently, so it doesn't have to hijack every family moment the way it has been. I'm wondering, when you imagine leaving here feeling "exactly the same," what would feeling even slightly different actually look like to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess feeling slightly different would be... maybe going to a family dinner and not spending the whole time fixating on the empty chair where she used to sit. Like, maybe being able to laugh at something without immediately feeling guilty about it, because it feels wrong to enjoy myself when she's not there anymore. But honestly, even as I say that, I'm not sure I actually believe it's possible right now.
therapist: What you just described — laughing without guilt, not being consumed by that empty chair — that's actually a really meaningful and specific hope, even if it feels out of reach right now. But as you said it, I noticed something that sounded almost like grief in your voice itself, a quietness that felt heavier than your words let on. I wonder if part of you is mourning not just her, but also the version of yourself that could enjoy those moments freely — does that resonate at all?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, that actually does resonate, more than I expected it to. It's like before she died, I just took it for granted that I could be happy at family things, and now that version of me feels kind of... gone too, or at least locked away somewhere. But I don't know, saying I'm "mourning a version of myself" sounds almost self-indulgent when she's the one who actually died — like, shouldn't this be about her, not me?
therapist: The way you just said that — softly, almost carefully, like you were afraid to take up too much space — makes me wonder if that idea of being "self-indulgent" is something you really believe, or something you're telling yourself to keep your own pain small. Grief isn't a competition, and mourning the loss of your own joy doesn't take anything away from how much she mattered. What do you think she would have said if she heard you dismiss your own hurt that way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: She would have hated hearing me talk like that, honestly — she was always the one telling me my feelings mattered and that I was too hard on myself. Thinking about that actually makes me want to cry, because it's like she'd be disappointed that I'm still doing the same thing even after losing her. But it also feels almost manipulative of me to use what she would have wanted as a reason to feel okay about my own grief, like I'm putting words in her mouth to make myself feel better.
therapist: It's so tender that you know her so well — that you can still hear her voice telling you your feelings matter, even now. And I'd gently push back on the word "manipulative," because drawing on what someone who loved you deeply believed about you isn't putting words in her mouth — it's letting her love still reach you. What if honoring what she saw in you is actually one of the most genuine ways you have left to stay connected to her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's a really beautiful way to put it, and part of me wants to hold onto that framing. But I also worry that if I start thinking about grief as a way to "stay connected" to her, I might use it as an excuse to never actually move forward — like, what if holding onto the sadness feels safer than risking losing that connection to her altogether? I don't know if that makes sense, but letting go even a little bit feels terrifying.
therapist: What you're describing makes complete sense — there's a real fear that moving forward means leaving her behind, like grief is the last thread still tying you to her. But I'd invite you to consider that the connection you have with her lives in so much more than the sadness — it's in the way you still know exactly what she'd say to you, in the values she passed on, in the love that's clearly still so present in how you talk about her. What if healing isn't about letting go of her, but about learning to carry her with you in a way that doesn't cost you so much?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That idea of carrying her with me rather than letting go — it actually feels a little less scary when you put it that way, like there's a difference between moving forward and moving away from her. But I guess my honest worry is that in the day-to-day reality of a family dinner, I won't be able to access that framing — it sounds good here, in this calm space, but when I'm sitting at that table and her chair is empty, I don't know if I'll be able to hold onto it. It feels like the kind of thing that makes sense intellectually but might just fall apart in the moment.
therapist: That worry is actually really wise and worth taking seriously — insight in a calm room and access to that insight in a painful moment are genuinely different skills, and it makes sense that one feels easier than the other right now. What we can work on together is building small, concrete anchors — things you can actually do or notice in that moment at the table — so the framing isn't just an idea but something you can reach for when the grief rushes in. Can you think of anything, even something tiny, that has ever helped you feel close to her in a way that felt more grounding than painful?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: There's this one thing — she had a really specific perfume she always wore, and sometimes I'll catch a similar scent somewhere and instead of making me fall apart, it actually makes me feel like she's nearby for a second. But I don't know how that translates to sitting at a dinner table, like I can't exactly bring a bottle of her perfume to Thanksgiving and sniff it in front of everyone without that being really strange. I guess I'm just not sure how to turn something that happens accidentally into something I can actually use on purpose.
therapist: What you just shared is actually really significant — you've already found something that connects you to her without breaking you apart, and that's not a small thing. You don't have to bring the bottle to the table; even something private, like a tiny amount on your wrist before you arrive, could be a quiet anchor that's just between you and her. It's worth exploring whether having that sensory thread with you might help you feel like she hasn't entirely left the room, even when her chair is empty.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually doesn't sound as strange as I was imagining — it's small enough that nobody else would even know, which makes it feel less embarrassing somehow. But I'd have to find out if her perfume is even still available to buy, and honestly I'm not sure I'm ready to go looking for it yet, because what if I find it and it just makes everything worse instead of better. I guess I'm a little afraid of testing something that feels fragile right now.
therapist: That instinct to protect something fragile is worth listening to — you don't have to rush toward the perfume, and there's no timeline here that requires you to be ready before you actually are. What's meaningful is that you can already imagine it as a possibility, which is different from where you were at the start of our conversation today. When you notice that fear of "making things worse," I'm curious — is that a pattern you recognize in other areas too, where protecting yourself from potential pain sometimes keeps you from things that might also help?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think that pattern is pretty familiar if I'm being honest — like, I've been avoiding calling some of my aunts since the funeral because I'm scared the conversation will just make me more sad, but then I also feel guilty and lonely because I haven't reached out. It's like I'm stuck in this loop where protecting myself from pain ends up creating a different kind of pain. I just don't know how to break that cycle without feeling like I'm forcing myself into something I'm not ready for.
therapist: You've just named something really important — that the very thing you're doing to feel safe is also the thing keeping you isolated, and that loop is exhausting to be caught in. In CBT we'd call this an avoidance cycle, where the short-term relief of not calling actually reinforces the fear and makes the next call feel even harder. I'm wondering, if you imagined the smallest possible version of reaching out — not a long emotional conversation, but maybe just a text to one aunt saying you've been thinking of her — does that feel any different than the full weight of what you've been dreading?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech
